data.title: UT students fire back after Republican's 'blatantly racist' post
data.description:
University of Texas at Austin (UT) students fired back Monday against a “blatantly racist” post from the Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner Bo French.

French posted an image over the weekend of UT students who were mostly South Asian with the caption: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

One student, Dhairya Gupta, shown in the images French shared, told The Dallas Morning News Monday that he was “having some enjoyment” during the game but “now it’s just people being blatantly racist toward us.”

Gupta and his friend Rahul Kodali, who was also in the images French posted, said they were both U.S. citizens. Gupta immigrated to the U.S. when he was 5 and gained citizenship in childhood while Kodali was born in New York before his family moved to the Dallas area. 

“Whether or not we are immigrants, that doesn’t change anything,” Kodali told the Dallas newspaper. “I’ve been an American my entire life.” 

Gupta continued that he “thought it was surprising that people are going out of their way to be racist on that.”

“They have people voting for them, and they’re not scared to say this kind of thing,” Gupta told the Dallas Morning News. “It’s becoming to the point where this kind of racism just isn’t looked down upon as much as it used to be — or it feels like that.” 

The incident has already been condemned by Texas GOP lawmakers – including Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas). 

“Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad,” Cornyn wrote on social platform X.

Texas state Rep. Lacey Hull (R) urged French to delete the post.

“This post breaks my heart,” she wrote on X. “I see college kids cheering on their football team. I see Texans.”

Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R) urged French to delete the post and said the candidate can oppose immigration policies “without demeaning people because of their race or ethnicity –– this post has crossed the line.”

French, despite the broad criticism, has not apologized for the post.

Asked by Dallas news outlet WFAA-TV in July if he regretted these remarks, French said he did not before adding, “Truth sounds like hate to those who hate the truth.”

data.title: Target opening new stores soon, with dozens more 'upcoming'
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Costco isn’t the only major retailer with a massive expansion plan in the works. Target is progressing toward its own growth goal with a slew of new openings set for October.

The Minnesota-based retailer previously announced plans to have over 300 new stores by 2035. It’s been well on its way all year, opening its 2,000th location in March. Based on Target’s calculations, most U.S. households can find a store within 10 miles of their doorsteps.

Eight communities will soon see a new Target open near them.

A spokesperson tells Nexstar the following stores are scheduled to open on October 11:

  • Tupelo, Mississippi
  • Bridgehampton, New York
  • Cookeville, Tennessee
  • Fort Worth-Chisholm Trail, Texas
  • Katy Heritage, Texas
  • Liberty Hill, Texas
  • Norfolk-Wards Corner, Virginia

Another store, replacing a shuttered Macy’s in Lima, Ohio, will open on November 8.

The Tupelo store is set to be the largest Target in Mississippi, covering roughly 148,000 square feet. The stores opening in Texas will be about the same size, according to Target, while the location opening in Bridgehampton will come in at around 90,000 square feet. The remaining stores will have footprints of about 128,000 square feet.

All of the new stores will also feature Starbucks Cafés.

These are the last of the more than 30 stores Target planned to open in 2026, but several more remain in the works.

According to Target’s website, there are more than 30 additional stores across 21 states slated to open eventually:

  • Chelsea, Alabama
  • Denver, Colorado
  • Monument, Colorado
  • Clearwater, Florida
  • Fort Lauderdale, Florida
  • Winter Haven, Florida
  • Covington, Georgia
  • Chubbuck, Idaho
  • Meridian, Idaho
  • Round Lake Beach, Illinois
  • Terre Haute, Indiana
  • Georgetown Commons, Kentucky
  • Denham Springs, Louisiana
  • Davison, Michigan
  • Farmington, Missouri
  • Albuquerque, New Mexico
  • Rego Center, New York
  • Fayetteville, North Carolina
  • Mebane, North Carolina
  • Fargo, North Dakota
  • Williston, North Dakota
  • Hermitage, Pennsylvania
  • Lexington, South Carolina
  • Newport/Rock Hill, South Carolina
  • Gallatin, Tennessee
  • Lebanon, Tennessee
  • Millington, Tennessee
  • Dripping Springs, Texas
  • Fate, Texas
  • Houston (Garden Oaks), Texas
  • San Antonio (Marbach), Texas
  • Farr West, Utah
  • Herriman, Utah
  • Lehi, Utah
  • Brown Deer, Wisconsin

Many of these stores, including Denver, Monument, Covington, Chubbuck, Meridian, Terre Haute, Hermitage, Gallatin, Dripping Springs, Herriman, Lehi, and Brown Deer, are expected to open in 2027, according to previous reports. The location in Chelsea may not open until 2028.

In Meridian, Winter Haven, Denham Springs, Davison, Fayetteville, Williston, Hermitage, Lexington, Newport, Farr West, Farmington, and Albuquerque, Target is set to anchor new or growing developments.

In others, Target is replacing former retail spaces, like an old Sears in Clearwater, a theater and office retailer in Fort Lauderdale, a vacant Kmart in Round Lake Beach, and a mall under redevelopment in Chubbuck.

data.title: When a return to the office is a return to sex-discrimination
data.description:
The sound returns with the commute: elevator chatter, side comments in the hallway, the meeting where an idea lands only after someone else repeats it. During the pandemic, remote settings muted many of these slights. New evidence shows that wasn’t a coincidence.  

A recent Organization Science study undertakes an analysis of everyday gender discrimination, finding that women experience far fewer gendered offenses when working remotely. As employers roll out return-to-office rules, the risk is clear: Mandates are not neutral. They can re-create the exact conditions that drive women out of roles, teams and entire fields.

Gender bias often hides in routine interactions. The Organization Science research found materially lower rates of everyday discrimination for women when remote, with the largest benefits for younger women and those working mostly with men. Their experiences improved sharply online, then worsened on-site, a pattern consistent with a less salient gender frame in virtual settings.  

The core takeaway is not that remote work is perfect — it is that location changes exposure to bias. Why? Physical proximity amplifies unstructured interactions where interruptions, offhand remarks and assignment-drift occur.  

A national poll on harassment found in-person employees more than twice as likely to experience sexual harassment as remote peers. When slights escalate, risk rises for companies as well. In fiscal 2024, the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission reported 88,531 new discrimination charges, up more than 9 percent year over year. That surge doesn’t prove causation from return-to-office mandates; it does underscore a compliance environment where re-exposing employees to higher-risk contexts is shortsighted.

Structured online workflows also narrow the aperture for bias. Virtual agendas, typed chat, and recorded decisions leave trails that make harder idea-stealing, selective credit and exclusion. Toronto’s Rotman School of Management describes remote work as a “protective shield” because it changes interaction patterns. Leaders who default to physical presence reintroduce unstructured spaces where bias thrives and documentation fades. For professionals charged with retention, engagement and legal stewardship, the office isn’t just a place. It’s a risk surface area. 

Mandates rarely land evenly. In the U.S., high-profile employers are hardening stance: Amazon is enforcing an on-site regime per its widely reported five-day mandate, complete with badge-tracking scrutiny. Even when other firms retain hybrid norms, like Meta’s steady status quo, the gravitational pull of stricter policies is real.

These rules collide with unequal caregiving and commute burdens. The Federal Reserve’s 2024 well-being report links employment decisions to child care constraints; mothers were more likely to report work impacts from care. Among adult caregivers, 67 percent struggle to balance jobs and care, according to one global analysis of U.S. workers. When you add uncompensated commute time and rigid arrival hours, the penalty compounds for women, who still carry disproportionate domestic labor.

Crucially, the preference data reinforces the equity case for flexibility. Women express stronger work-from-home preferences in post-pandemic surveys, including an IZA analysis of data from the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes. When mandates ignore that asymmetry, they don’t just raise attrition risk; they tilt opportunity away from a talent pool that has already asked clearly for flexibility. For leaders, that is both a recruiting problem and a brand problem. 

The strongest case for a return to work in the office rests on development, mentoring and innovation. But here, the evidence points to nuance, not dogma. A National Bureau of Economic Research paper on proximity among software engineers shows real trade-offs: Proximity to coworkers increases long-run human capital development but reduces short-term output. The solution is not necessarily to shift fully on-site; it is to design for intentional proximity where it matters, while preserving flexibility that cuts bias and attrition. 

First, protect flexibility as a default, not a perk. Research shows hybrid as a stable equilibrium, and women’s stronger preference for it is well documented. Second, import remote discipline into the office. Codify agendas, timeboxed turns and written briefs to curb interruptions and credit-theft. Third, measure exposure and outcomes. If harassment reports and bias incidents spike with more on-site days, treat location as a controllable variable and adjust.  

Finally, be candid about the home front. Even as companies promise equal opportunity, women still perform more household labor. Policies that ignore this reality are not neutral — in fact, they redistribute friction toward women. Flexible scheduling, predictable team anchor days, and transparent assignment systems create access to the same developmental reps that proximity can offer, without forcing daily exposure to the most biased moments of office life. Leaders who tie promotion readiness to output, documented scope and peer-reviewed impact, rather than hallway-time, close the visibility gap that a return-to-office policy otherwise widens.

The evidence is consistent across sources: Remote and hybrid work reduce the day-to-day slights that wear women down, whereas rigid on-site rules reignite those frictions and stack penalties related to care, commute and safety. Development matters, but it does not require daily presence. It requires intent.  

For the best results, firms should arrange to keep the bias-reducing benefits of remote work, paired with scheduled, purposeful proximity for coaching and creativity. And they should judge performance by outcomes. Do that, and you protect equity without sacrificing growth. Ignore it, and you will keep losing the very talent you claim you want to develop. 

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results” and “ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators.”

data.title: Democrats urge RFK Jr. to scrap proposed Head Start overhaul
data.description:
Democrats are pressing Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to scrap a proposed overhaul of the Head Start program, warning the changes would weaken services for thousands of families nationwide.

The proposed rule, dubbed “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs,” would “rescind and replace” the Head Start Program Performance Standards to “reduce regulatory burden,” “eliminate duplication with statutory requirements” and “reinforce state and local authority,” among other things, according to the Federal Register. 

But in a letter to Kennedy, members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus argued that HHS’s proposed rule would “strip the Head Start Program Performance Standards (HSPPS) of more than 90 percent of its standards, likely taking away vital services from children and families.”

“It eliminates and substantially weakens federal requirements governing early learning, health, mental health, and dental services, safety standards, family engagement and family social services, and other services that have defined Head Start for six decades,” they wrote. 

The lawmakers said the proposed rule would eliminate a federal requirement that children be supervised at all times, reduce mandatory annual training on preventing abuse and neglect and repeal prohibitions on corporal punishment, shaming, humiliation and seclusion. 

It would also “require Head Start instruction to be conducted in English, with an exception for Tribal programs,” a move that lawmakers argue would weaken dual-language learning.

The letter had 70 signers as of Monday and is led by Democratic Women’s Caucus Chair Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), as well as Reps. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.), and Kristen McDonald-Rivet (D-Mich.).

“Head Start ensures our most vulnerable kids have access to the care, nutrition, and health services they need in those early years. I am proud to be a voice for the parents, like me, who are enraged by the anti-family, backward agenda of this administration,” Pettersen said in a statement. “I will fight every effort by Trump to dismantle this program and work to protect Colorado families and kids across the country.”

data.title: Watch live: Bessent faces House questions on economy
data.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will testify Tuesday before the House Financial Services Committee on the state of the U.S. financial system, as President Trump’s economic agenda faces scrutiny amid the Iran war and tariff battles.

Trump’s latest trade war with Canada, the 10-year Treasury bond yield and federal deficit, affordability concerns as the midterms inch closer and rising energy prices tied to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz are likely to come up in the hearing.

Bessent has defended the president’s moves, particularly in the Middle East. The Trump administration also threatened to issue new sanctions on nations that continue to support Iran in the ongoing conflict.

The event is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. EDT.

data.title: Watch live: House Republicans give remarks amid AI turmoil
data.description:
House Republican leaders will speak with reporters Tuesday morning as calls mount for more transparency around artificial intelligence and implementing guardrails around the rapidly developing technology.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dismissed the idea of swiftly adding regulations on the AI industry, despite tech leaders’ warnings of the dangers of the technology if development is not slowed down. President Trump has also called the alarm a “hoax.”

data.title: McMahon has a chance to lock in charter school opportunities
data.description:
Recent primary elections delivered a reminder of how temporary good policy can be. A bevy of candidates competing for congressional seats oppose providing public support for expansive education opportunities outside traditional education, including the 35 year-old reform called charter schools, which has historically enjoyed bi-partisan congressional support.

And in an age where student proficiency is widely understood to be in crisis, the nation can ill-afford to neglect any opportunity to improve it.

That is where Education Secretary Linda McMahon, working with Congress, has an opportunity to lock in efforts to improve student achievement. A new state-by-state scorecard reveals that states with strong charter school laws not only improve achievement but are responsible for the majority of the new and growing innovative public schools that chartering codifies in state law.

Understanding that opportunity, the Congress created in 1997 an initiative to incentivize states passing laws that give teachers, parents, and community leaders the freedom to build and run their own public schools.

Sponsored by the late Rep. Frank Riggs (R-Calif.) in the House and Sen. Joe Lieberman (D-Conn.) in the Senate, it was signed into law by President Bill Clinton. It created Public Charter School Grant Program at a time when more than two dozen states had already enacted laws making charter schools possible.

Federal start-up funding was supposed to add momentum by rewarding states that encouraged the creation of charters and gave them a level of independence and freedom to operate. And it worked that way for a while, until overzealous lawmakers, regulators and even some charter school advocates backed changes, and the competition for limited dollars became more about meeting various regulatory benchmarks than supporting operational freedom.

For example, Connecticut, which ranks at the bottom of the scorecard, received $24.5 million in 2022. Although those funds did pass through to one charter school, the state also funded an agency whose leadership is hostile to charter schools opening and denies charter schools equitable funding.

California received the largest grant in 2024, despite having passed a law that restricts charter schools to district approvals. Rhode Island, which earns a D-minus on the scorecard and ranks 45th nationally, has a statutory cap on new charter schools and one of the most centralized approval processes in the country.

Although great leaders can change the trajectory of non-entitlement-related education programs more easily with funding decisions, equality of public support for public charter schools should not be subject to political winds.

Since she has been in leadership, Secretary Linda McMahon’s department has made decisions more aligned to the law’s intent. Major awards in fiscal 2025 went to states that have maintained and even improved their strong charter school laws over time, such as Ohio, North Carolina, and Iowa.

But here’s the rub: These decisions are based on who is in charge and on regulators, not on the original intent of the law. Without codifying the law’s original intent, the states and the schools themselves are subjected to choices that a future secretary or future legislative majority could reverse without changing a single word of the law.

Meanwhile, three pro-charter members of Congress have all introduced bills this year to isolate and favor certain kinds of programs as part of the overall charter school grant program. Unfortunately, they are undermining their own intended result — more and better charter school laws at the state level that foster more and better education opportunities for kids.

That is why the principles of the original law need to become a requirement, not a choice, ensuring that Washington is not telling states how to spend their funds, but giving them a clear pathway to receive funds if they demonstrate their law meets the proven measures of what makes a great law.

My organization’s national charter law ranking and scorecard is a great instruction manual that can help build the right standard directly into how the charter school grant competition is scored and structured. It identifies what a strong charter law actually looks like — independent authorizers, real operational autonomy, funding that follows students and room for good schools to grow. State by state, it points out what is still missing.

Before federal dollars go out the door, the Education Department should return to the question Congress intended it to ask in 1997: Does this state’s law actually let charter schools be charter schools? The scorecard provides the answer, but Congress needs to ensure the principles are codified.

In addition to executing in this way, McMahon can use her bully pulpit to champion states that have done the hard work of building strong charter laws. She can also press those that haven’t, starting with her home state, to remove the barriers keeping schools from opening and growing, and make sure Washington rewards freedom rather than bureaucracy.

Jeanne Allen is founder and CEO of the Center for Education Reform and author of “The Education Avengers: Why and How A New Class of Heroes Is Fighting America’s Biggest Battle.”

data.title: Ossoff: 'Compromised' Trump won't regulate AI
data.description:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) on Monday said President Trump will likely not heed calls from technology leaders to implement guardrails on the development of artificial intelligence (AI) because of his family’s investments in the industry. 

The Georgia Democrat pointed to venture capitalist firm 1789 Capital, where Trump’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, and its investments in AI.

“They’ve invested heavily in AI labs. They’ve invested heavily in data centers,” Ossoff told MS Now’s Lawrence O’Donnell. “So, the first family has a financial stake in this industry, and as a result, the president of the United States is compromised.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The president earlier Monday waived aside concerns raised by current and former employees of AI companies about the potential dangers of the emerging tech.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A has that, in spades!” he wrote Monday Truth Social post. 

The criticism follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s announcement of a plan to slow the pace of AI development to allow for proper safeguards to be developed and implemented. 

Trump, who is set to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week in Washington, cited U.S. competition with China on AI development in a separate post as justification to move forward with new technologies.

“President Xi, of China, just announced that China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future,” he wrote, calling the worries about the dangers of the technology “a HOAX.”

“AI, and Data Centers, will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History ­­— Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet,” the president continued. “It will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!”

AI is expected to play a part in the discussions between the two leaders at the upcoming bilateral summit. 

Xi is reportedly bringing a large delegation of Chinese business leaders with him to the U.S., although it is unclear which industries will be represented by this group, according to Reuters. 

When Trump visited Beijing for a bilateral summit in May, he brought a group of American business and technology executives, including Apple CEO Tim Cook and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. 

Ossoff, who is running for reelection for his Senate seat in Georgia, called on voters to make their discontent with the president’s stance on AI known at the ballot box. 

“We already know that Donald Trump is a dangerously corrupt and incompetent man,” the senator said. “The question is what we’re going to do about it.”

data.title: With Lonnie Bunch's ouster, Trump chills free speech at the Smithsonian
data.description:
The Smithsonian Institution is a group of museums, education and research centers, created by Congress as a trust in 1846 “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge.” About 62 percent of its funding comes from the federal government. The Smithsonian is supposed to be independent of the executive branch. A bipartisan board of regents runs the show. 

The Smithsonian’s first Black chieftain, Lonnie G. Bunch III 73, announced his retirement last week after more than seven years in the institution’s top job. Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, lauded Bunch for “excellence in the telling of our nation’s story,” stating that the Smithsonian had “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.”  

The truth is Trump forced Bunch out of his job, heralding a tectonic shift in institutional purpose.  

Over nearly 40 years in various roles at the Smithsonian, Bunch proved himself as an effective advocate and diplomat, and an incredible fundraiser. As the institution’s guiding spirit, he was also a forceful voice on race, particularly after the 2017 Charlottesville incident and George Floyd’s 2020 Minneapolis murder. 

Bunch is a man of considerable soft-spoken warmth. I met him in New York last June when he was honored by the conservative Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History for his contributions to history, education and scholarship. He left an indelible impression. The son of two teachers, his love of history was palpable as he said eloquently, “there is nothing more powerful than a people, than a nation, steeped in its history. And there’s nothing more noble than honoring all our ancestors by remembering.”  

What obviously led to Bunch’s abrupt resignation was Trump on his case. Out of some perverse desire for political cleansing of artistic expression, Trump waged a chilling campaign on the Smithsonian to purge what he called “improper ideology,”  going so far as to threaten the institution’s federal funding and challenge its autonomy. 

Bunch told the New York Times it was not the Trump freeze-out that spurred his departure, but admitted that at times, his role had been “stressful”. 

“When you’re Black in America, you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right?” he said. “You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table.” 

Trump’s drive to gut the Smithsonian began in March 2025 with an executive order that accused the institution of spouting a “divisive” and “race centered” message. The White House subsequently identified exhibits it found objectionable, principally targeting discussions of race, slavery, immigration and transgender identity. 

The sparks flew further in May 2025 when Trump said he had fired Kim Sajet, longtime director of the National Portrait Gallery, calling her highly partisan and a supporter of diversity, equity and inclusion. The Smithsonian’s regents pushed back. After a tense meeting, they publicly affirmed that personnel decisions belonged to Bunch, with oversight by the board. Sajet resigned four days later, saying her departure was the best way to serve the institution.  

Pressure soon expanded beyond personnel. Trump went ballistic posting on social media in August 2025 that the institution “is OUT OF CONTROL,” and only discusses “how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been.” 

“We have the “HOTTEST” Country in the World, and we want people to talk about it, including in our Museums,” he added.  

This spring, Bunch said he was proud of what the Smithsonian had achieved under his leadership despite the barrage of Trump attacks. “Nothing can take that away,” he said. “So, I’m trying to make sure I don’t let this moment steal my joy.”

The White House next produced a July 4 report about the National Museum of American History that accused its director of “radical activist ideology” and charges the museum with undermining “faith in American institutions.” The board called for its 21 museums to review their content for partisanship or bias. But the administration began its own review of exhibitions, wall text and social media to assess “tone, historical framing and alignment with American ideals.”  

After the report, the salvos continued. Museum director Anthea M. Hartig came under fire at two congressional hearings. Trump ordered posting of warning signs to convey his view that the museum did not accurately reflect American history. The signs never appeared.

Later, the White House escalated again, with a 162-page report accusing the National Museum of American History of portraying the American story as one of “regret, tragedy, and shame.”  

Bunch, who generally avoided publicly confronting Trump, forcefully pushed back. He told Smithsonian employees the report was “not a fair characterization” of the museum and said its work remained driven by “scholarship, accuracy, and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America’s story.” 

“America is not afraid of its own history,” Bunch said. “My job is always to help the Smithsonian tell complicated stories that really allow us to understand the fullness of the American experience.” The institution’s 180-year-old history is “a reservoir…for understanding of science, of history, of art.”  

“For me, it is really building on the Smithsonian’s long history of saying, ‘No matter what, we will be independent.’”  

Bunch plans to depart by the end of the year.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.
